claim: The C2/C3 melange-coverage gap in line 40 is not just an elicitation-quality shortfall but a terminal-gate integrity gap: the unvalidated condition string (finding f-011) is the sole trigger for the kernel-gated close sequence under candidate (a), and C2/C3 — the likely majority tier — gets neither melange nor any other check on it.

Every terminal-gate candidate — the three in the doc and the additional shapes this probe was asked to surface (lease/heartbeat, escrowed close, successor-proposal-as-obligation-object) — locates the successor-proposal obligation inside the SAME execution path as the closing session, with no standing party independent of administrator turnover accountable for the obligation existing at all. If that session dies between goal-fulfilled and next-goal-fired, the obligation evaporates with nothing else positioned to notice.

claim: Candidate (a) (two-layer ordered close) names no lock/lease/single-writer mechanism, so two sessions attached to the same goal can each independently kernel-gate the terminal sequence.

Intercore already contains two tested, durable single-point-of-no-return primitives (sentinel.Store.Check DB-transactional atomic claim; lock.Manager filesystem lease with staleness/heartbeat detection) that are mechanistically the 'lease/heartbeat model' PRIORITY-1 asked to be surfaced, and the terminal-gate open question proposes new shapes from scratch without referencing either.

The only party that confirms a goal's terminal condition was met is the same Haiku evaluator/session that ran the loop being judged; for C1-C3 goals (the likely majority per the settled melange-coverage-gap fact) there is no second-party check at all, unlike the formation ritual which explicitly requires a second party (agent + user) before ratification.

Claim (2) holds and claim (1) is a code-reading error, not an irreducible taste call: sentinel.Store.Check has no owner/PID/release semantics and cannot distinguish 'no recent activity' from 'the tending session died' — it is a pure atomic interval-throttle (Sentinel{Name, ScopeID, LastFired}, no Release method anywhere in the file). lock.Manager IS a genuine lease/heartbeat primitive (Lock{Owner, PID, Host, Created}, Release with ErrNotOwner check, tryBreakStale combining staleness threshold with pidAlive() liveness detection). Claim (1)'s error is bundling both primitives together as 'mechanistically the lease/heartbeat model' — only lock.Manager qualifies. Claim (2)'s mechanism risk is also verified: sentinel, not lock.Manager, is the primitive already wired into the goal-cadence Stop-hook path (auto-stop-actions.sh:142, intercore_sentinel_check_or_legacy "goal_cadence_throttle"), so a terminal-gate design built 'by analogy to what's already there' would reach for sentinel and inherit its blindness to died-mid-work sessions — exactly the failure mode the settled facts already flag (successor-proposal obligation evaporates if the closing session dies).

lock.Manager, intercore's one candidate lease/heartbeat primitive, has no fencing/generation token and a 5s default staleness window against a necessarily multi-LLM-call terminal sequence, so a stale-lock break during that sequence lets two officiants each complete a fully witnessed (file-written) close of the same Goal with no ledger of which is canonical.

sentinel.Store.Check is a single-column (LastFired), session-scoped, fire-once-per-interval throttle with no step/ordinal concept, so naively reusing it for goal-close would satisfy neither the transaction parent's per-step-checkpoint requirement nor the rite parent's witnessed-completion requirement, and its one existing call site is keyed by SESSION_ID rather than goal ID.

claim: CONFIRMED: the ritual states the Haiku-evaluator/surfaced-output-only/≤4000-char constraint precisely (line 13) but describes no step anywhere — at any stakes tier, including C4/C5 melange — that validates a drafted completion condition against that constraint before ratification.

The successor-proposal-as-separate-obligation-object shape PRIORITY-1 asked to be scored relocates the fencing requirement onto a new object's CREATE step without inheriting any mechanism to enforce single-witness creation, so two sessions on the same goal reaching terminal conditions near-simultaneously can each independently create an obligation record, reproducing the double-witness defect one level down.

Finding (1) holds over finding (2): sentinel.Store.Check and lock.Manager are not mechanistically equivalent, and (2)'s bundling of them as an interchangeable 'lease/heartbeat' pair overstates sentinel's fitness for terminal-gate reuse and risks a by-analogy design reaching for the wrong (already Stop-hook-wired) primitive. (2)'s narrower point — a real, tested lease primitive (lock.Manager) already exists unreferenced in the doc — survives and should carry into the melange candidate list.

The Goal entity's close evidence is described only as coarse ('accumulates close evidence'), with no per-step completion record, so a crash mid-sequence is unrecoverable and indistinguishable from not-started.

claim: Intercore's only existing liveness-adjacent primitive (the sentinel package) is a fire-once-per-interval throttle with no holder identity, renewal, or release semantics — not a lease. A lease/heartbeat terminal-gate candidate built by analogy to it (the natural move, since it's already wired into the goal-cadence Stop-hook path) inherits throttle semantics and cannot distinguish 'no recent activity' from 'the tending session died.'

New insight the contradiction exposed: narrowing claim (1) to lock.Manager alone reveals it is also not a drop-in fit — it is process-local (filesystem locks under /tmp/intercore/locks, 5-second default staleness, PID-liveness checked via a local pidAlive call) rather than distributed/cross-host, tuned for short-lived command-level mutual exclusion rather than a goal that spans many runs/sessions possibly across machines and days. The doc's terminal-gate open question cites neither primitive at all, so the melange round has no existing-primitive anchor for the lease/heartbeat shape PRIORITY 1 asked to be surfaced.

'Recommended option first' interview ordering runs against the ritual's own stated comparative-advantage premise (user's judgment should steer selection) with no feedback loop to detect anchoring drift, despite the project already having a directly reusable pattern for this (interspect drift audits).

claim: The doc's own open question about whether melange reviews the charter doc versus what the kernel gates on (the fields) admits these may be two different objects with no reconciliation step, so even a full C4/C5 melange pass may not actually validate the literal condition string handed to /goal.

The charter's founder-authored acceptance criteria are framed as binding every subsequent run, but the doc never states whether they are editable after ratification, and if so what re-ratifies them (a second melange pass, silent unilateral patch by whichever run notices a gap, or a wholly new Goal).

Even lock.Manager, the correctly-identified lease-shaped primitive, does not clear the bar a terminal-gate close sequence actually needs: it has no fencing/generation token and only a 5-second DefaultStaleAge, sized for short filesystem-lock holds rather than a multi-step sequence spanning several LLM calls (verify-against-charter -> reflect+compound -> next-goal proposal per candidate (a)). Pointing at lock.Manager as prior art is necessary corrective guidance but not sufficient design guidance.

The undecided charter storage shape (entity fields vs. companion doc vs. both) creates two independent attestation artifacts with no stated authority or synchronization rule, risking a state where the doc says ratified and the kernel-gating fields disagree.
